Export controls aim to prevent advanced AI hardware from reaching foreign adversaries that could use it for military or surveillance purposes.

entries.text: Researchers report a rise in ransomware incidents as attackers incorporate artificial intelligence into their methods.
The number of alleged attacks on public leak sites reached nearly 3,000 over the summer, a 20‑40 % increase since spring.
Experts say the growth is driven by more international campaigns, with the United States remaining steady but still high.
The surge is linked to AI use in parts of the ransomware chain, such as crafting more convincing phishing emails and automating negotiation messages.
Allan Liska of Recorded Future notes that while most groups remain human‑run, they are experimenting heavily with large language models, which could accelerate changes in tactics.
Cynthia Kaiser, former FBI cyber deputy director, highlights that the international dimension of attacks is the most novel aspect and attributes part of the increase to AI‑enabled capabilities.
Ransomware has been a top cyber threat for a decade, targeting institutions and indirectly affecting individuals.
Traditional ransomware relies on manual steps, but AI tools lower the barrier for creating tailored lures and handling victim communication, making attacks faster and potentially more widespread.
problems: model check: Source mentions AI aiding phishing and negotiation but does not describe traditional ransomware as manual or claim AI lowers the overall barrier and speeds attacks.

entries.text: On September 27 US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy announced the AI‑infused air‑traffic management system called SMART on X, calling it a “GAME CHANGER” and saying it would save time and cut delays.

Three weeks later, on Friday the 13th, the FAA issued a national groundstop that disrupted airline schedules, and officials said there was no evidence of a cyberattack or that SMART caused the communications failure.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said officials could not yet rule out an AI fault.

The SMART system is part of a broader AI aviation push, illustrated by a pilotless 3,200‑mile Cessna Caravan flight that departed Buchanan Field Airport in Concord, California and landed at Dare County Regional Airport in North Carolina, stopping at Shaw Air Force Base in South Carolina and Fort Worth en route.
Joby Aviation reported a safety pilot remained aboard but never intervened, marking a milestone for unmanned commercial flight.
The flight navigated busy airspace and avoided storms without human control, showing AI can handle complex routing tasks.
Air traffic control has traditionally relied on proven, human‑centric technology because safety is paramount.
Recent AI introductions aim to improve efficiency, but industry veterans warn that rapid, untested changes could introduce new risks.
The mixed reaction reflects a tension between potential economic benefits and concerns over reliability and safety in a sector that historically favors caution.
